title: ISC U1·W3 — Systems Development & Change Management (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — building and changing systems safely

New systems and changes to existing ones are where risk concentrates: a poorly built ERP or an untested change can corrupt data, break controls, or halt operations. The systems development life cycle (SDLC) and disciplined change management govern how Meridian Building Group acquires, builds, tests, and modifies the systems that run its job-cost and billing. This week covers the phases, the testing and conversion strategies, the project governance, and the controls that keep development from becoming the weakest link.

The systems development life cycle

The SDLC structures development into phases: planning (define the need, feasibility, and business case), analysis (gather and document requirements), design (specify the system and controls), development (build or configure), testing, implementation (deploy and convert), and maintenance. Crucially, controls and security must be designed in from the analysis and design phases — bolting them on later is costly and weaker. Each phase produces documentation and approvals, creating an auditable trail of decisions.

Requirements and design

The early phases determine success. Analysis captures what the business needs — functional requirements, data, reports, and the controls the system must enforce — with strong user involvement so the system fits the work. Design translates requirements into specifications: the data model, processes, interfaces, and the input/processing/output controls from Week 2. A choice arises between building custom software, buying a packaged solution, or adopting cloud/SaaS — each with different control and vendor-oversight implications. Getting requirements right is the cheapest place to prevent defects.

Testing

Disciplined testing validates the system before it goes live, in layers: unit testing (individual components), integration testing (components working together), system testing (the whole system against requirements), and user acceptance testing (UAT) — where business users confirm the system meets their needs before approval. Testing uses test data in a non-production environment, never live data without safeguards. Inadequate testing is a leading cause of failed implementations, so the test plan and its sign-offs are key controls in the SDLC.

Implementation and conversion strategies

Going live requires choosing a conversion approach, each trading risk against cost. Parallel conversion runs the old and new systems simultaneously until the new one is proven — safest but most expensive. Pilot conversion deploys to one location or unit first. Phased conversion rolls out in stages by module or function. Direct ("big-bang") cutover switches entirely at once — cheapest but riskiest, since there is no fallback if the new system fails. The choice depends on the system's criticality and the organization's risk tolerance.

Data conversion and migration

Moving data from the old system to the new — data conversion/migration — is a high-risk, often underestimated step. Data must be cleansed (duplicates, errors, inconsistent formats fixed), mapped from old fields to new, migrated, and then reconciled (record counts and control totals tied from source to target) to prove completeness and accuracy. A migration that silently drops or corrupts records carries the error into every future report. Reconciliation and a verified cutover are the controls that make conversion trustworthy.

Development methodologies and project governance

Development follows a methodology. Waterfall moves sequentially through the phases with heavy upfront documentation — predictable but inflexible. Agile develops iteratively in short cycles (sprints) with continuous user feedback — adaptive but requiring discipline to keep controls and documentation current. Either way, project governance — a sponsor, defined scope, budget and schedule tracking, risk management, and steering-committee oversight — keeps the project aligned and prevents the scope creep and cost overruns that sink IT projects. Governance is what turns a methodology into a controlled outcome.

Change management and post-implementation

Once live, the system enters maintenance, where change management (Week 2) governs every modification — authorized, tested in a separate environment, approved, documented, and migrated by someone other than the developer, with version control tracking what changed. A post-implementation review evaluates whether the system met its objectives and budget and captures lessons learned. Patch management keeps software current against vulnerabilities. These ongoing controls ensure the system stays reliable and secure long after go-live — development discipline does not end at implementation.

Documentation and system flowcharts

Throughout the SDLC, documentation is both a control and a deliverable: requirements specifications, design documents, test plans and results, user manuals, and operations runbooks. System and data-flow documentation — flowcharts, data-flow diagrams, and entity-relationship diagrams — lets analysts, users, and auditors understand how data moves and where controls sit. Strong documentation supports the experienced-auditor standard from AUD (someone with no prior connection can understand the system), enables maintenance, and reduces dependence on the original developers. A system no one but its author understands is itself a risk.

Acquiring versus building, and vendor selection

Many organizations buy rather than build. Acquiring software follows its own disciplined process: define requirements, issue a request for proposal (RFP), evaluate vendors on functionality, cost, support, and financial stability, and assess the controls — including the vendor's SOC report for a hosted solution. The contract should specify control responsibilities, data ownership, and exit terms. Whether built or bought, the same governance applies: the system must meet requirements, enforce controls, and be implemented and converted under the disciplines covered this week — the source of the software changes the procurement steps, not the control objectives.

Feasibility, the business case, and outsourced development

Before building, the planning phase establishes feasibility — technical, operational, economic (cost-benefit), and scheduling — and a business case that justifies the investment and defines success criteria; a steering-committee gate at each phase decides whether to proceed, revise, or cancel before more is spent. Skipping this is how organizations build systems no one needed. When development itself is outsourced to a vendor or offshore team, the organization retains responsibility for requirements, acceptance testing, and control design, and must manage the added risks of code quality, intellectual property, and data security in the vendor's hands. Governance over the project does not transfer with the coding work — the organization still owns the outcome and its controls.

CMA bridge

When MBG implements a new job-cost or ERP system, the conversion strategy and the data-migration reconciliation decide whether the CFO can trust the opening balances. A botched migration corrupts the very WIP and cost data the CMA program analyzes — which is why the SDLC's testing and reconciliation controls matter directly to the finance function.

Practice and recap

  1. Sequence the SDLC (planning → analysis → design → development → testing → implementation → maintenance) and design controls in from the start.
  2. Test in layers (unit, integration, system, UAT) using test data in a non-production environment.
  3. Choose a conversion strategy by risk: parallel (safest), pilot, phased, direct cutover (riskiest); reconcile data migration source-to-target.
  4. Govern projects (sponsor, scope, budget, risk) under waterfall or agile; apply change management, version control, and post-implementation review in maintenance.

Recap: the SDLC runs from planning and analysis through design, development, testing, implementation, and maintenance, with controls designed in early; testing proceeds in layers (unit, integration, system, UAT) on non-production data; conversion strategies trade risk for cost — parallel is safest, direct cutover riskiest — and data migration must be cleansed, mapped, and reconciled source-to-target; and disciplined project governance, version control, post-implementation review, and ongoing change/patch management keep the system reliable after go-live.

flashcards.back: Planning → analysis → design → development → testing → implementation → maintenance. Controls and security must be designed in from analysis/design, not bolted on later.
Unit (components) → integration (components together) → system (whole vs requirements) → user acceptance testing (UAT, business users approve). Use test data in a non-production environment.
Parallel (run both — safest, costliest) → pilot (one site) → phased (by module) → direct/big-bang cutover (switch at once — cheapest, riskiest, no fallback).
Cleanse, map old→new fields, migrate, then RECONCILE record counts/control totals source-to-target to prove completeness and accuracy.
Waterfall: sequential, heavy upfront docs, predictable but inflexible. Agile: iterative sprints with continuous user feedback, adaptive but needs discipline for controls/docs.
Custom build, packaged software, or cloud/SaaS — each with different control design and vendor-oversight (SOC report) implications.
After go-live, evaluate whether the system met objectives/budget and capture lessons learned; patch management keeps software current against vulnerabilities.
Sponsor, defined scope, budget/schedule tracking, risk management, steering-committee oversight — prevents scope creep and overruns.

questions.q: Internal controls in a new system should be:
choices: Designed in from the analysis/design phases
questions.explain: Designing controls in early is cheaper and stronger than bolting them on later.

questions.q: User acceptance testing (UAT) is performed by:
choices: Business users confirming the system meets their needs
questions.explain: UAT is the business users' validation that the system meets requirements before approval.

questions.q: Which conversion strategy is the SAFEST but most expensive?
questions.explain: Parallel runs old and new systems together until the new one is proven — safest, costliest.

questions.q: The riskiest conversion approach, with no fallback, is:
questions.explain: Direct cutover switches entirely at once; if the new system fails there is no fallback.

questions.q: After migrating data to a new system, the key control is to:
choices: Reconcile record counts and control totals source-to-target
questions.explain: Reconciliation proves the migration was complete and accurate.

choices: Iterative sprints with continuous user feedback
A single sequential pass with no feedback
questions.explain: Agile develops iteratively with frequent feedback; waterfall is sequential.

questions.q: Production migration of a program change should be performed by:
questions.explain: Segregating development from migration prevents unauthorized or untested code from going live.
